text:
Design a fraud detection system. That's the classic machine learning system design prompt. Now it's just as often: design an assistant over our documents. Or: this LLM feature is too slow and too expensive. Fix it. These videos cover both kinds: what every ML round still asks, and what large language models, LLMs, added.

Expect three rounds: coding, ML concepts, and ML system design. Across them, interviewers probe four areas. ML fundamentals: supervised and unsupervised learning, over- and underfitting, regularization, metrics and leakage. Coding: data structures and algorithms, plus NumPy and pandas. System design: training and serving pipelines, feature stores, batch or online inference, monitoring and drift. And em-el-ops: reproducibility, versioning data and models, CI CD, latency and cost. The track adds pages on statistics, deep learning, and NLP and LLMs, and each of those gets a part too.

Classical ML didn't leave when LLMs arrived: bias and variance, leakage, metrics and a coding round are all still asked. What LLMs added is four things. Application design: retrieval, prompting, tool use, guardrails and fallbacks, drawn as a system with budgets for latency and cost. Inference economics: why generation is slow, where the GPU memory goes, and which lever buys what. Evaluation with no single right answer: building a test set, trusting or distrusting an automated judge, and tying offline scores to online outcomes. And judgment about when not to use an LLM at all. Some companies also run coding rounds with an AI assistant allowed, so ask the recruiter about each round.
